To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the up regulation in VDRs during diabetes may be unique for the intestine and may be related to the hyperplasia of the intestinal tissue.

1) diabetes is characterized by up-regulation of intestinal VDR, 2) this occurs despite low plasma 1.25(OH) 2D 3 levels and 3) this may be related to the hyperplasia observed in the diabetic intestine.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the regulation of vitamin D receptor expression in intestine and kidney in streptozototocin diabetic animals.
the regulation of vitamin D receptors in streptozotcin-induced diabetes.
the role of vitamin D in the pathophysiology of diabetes mellitus.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
diabetes is a disease of intestinal VDR regulation and that the up regulation is associated with hyperplasia and may be related to the compensatory growth of the small intestine.
the intestinal compensatory growth during untreated diabetes was not related to 1,25 (OH)2D3.
diabetes induced compensatory intestinal growth was associated with up-regulation of intestinal VDR, but that this up-regulation was insufficient to prevent a low circulating 1.25(OH)D3.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
diabetes induced compensatory growth of the small intestine and kidney, but not thymus, and that diabetes up regulated VDRs in the intestine and kidney but not in the thymus.
the up-regulation of intestinal VDR during untreated diabetes may not be related to compensatory growth, but to hyperplasia of the small intestine.
diabetes causes intestinal and renal compensatory growth and that this is associated with increased VDR numbers in intestine but not in kidney.
The main takeaway from our work is that
diabetes is associated with compensatory growth of intestine and kidneys and that the up regulation VDRs during diabetes appears to be unique to intestine.
the up regulation in VDRs during diabetes is not a generalized response, but is unique to the intestine.
the intestinal compensatory growth during untreated diabetes is not due to increased 1,25 (OH)2D3 production by the kidneys, but rather to the up regulation of intestinal vitamin D receptors.
